e-8743.knowledge_point: Calculating the Curl of a Vector Field
e-8743.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F} = y\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j} - 2z\,\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf{F}$ at the point  $\left(-1,0,2\right).$
e-8743.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}+R\,\mathbf{k}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the curl of $\mathbf F$ is the vector field given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108829/assets/888b12c4f687dba1199a82d7e3a5e6897e7599ea812753423de5a23ffd756888.png)

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ y & {x}^{2} & -2z\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(y)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)]k \\  & =(0-0)i-(0-0)j+(2x-1)k \\  & =(2x-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm {curl}\, \mathbf{F}$ at the point $\left(-1,0,2\right),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(-1,0,2) & =(2(-1)-1)\,k=-3\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9556.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Curl of a Vector Field
e-9556.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = e^{x+y} \, \mathbf{i} + 3xy \, \mathbf{j}.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
e-9556.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf{i} + Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $\mathbf{F}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy)-\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}) \\  & =3y-{e}^{x+y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(-1,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(-1,1)} & =3(1)-{e}^{-1+1} \\  & =3-{e}^{0} \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

e-8929.knowledge_point: Interpreting the Curl of a Vector Field
e-8929.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108829/assets/71c58bf1b0fe4259ac50633a457f6a76639c0a0c188b66cce5e0fc3c7e5b0329.png)

 

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z),$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is independent of $z,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \mathbf 0$

- $\textrm{curl}\, \mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0$

- $\mathbf F$ is irrotational

- $\textrm{curl}\, \mathbf F$ points in the positive $z$-direction.
e-8929.worked_solution:
Recall that $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $\mathbf F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq  \mathbf 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F =  \mathbf 0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108829/assets/86aee33cdfa96ac0a61468cc9657e791e399f31c024cdbc3a932193dc897d534.png)

If $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F = \mathbf 0$ everywhere in $\mathbb R^3$, we say that $\mathbf F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is false, whereas statement II is true. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate counterclockwise. Therefore, $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0.$

- Statements III is false. Since $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F \neq \mathbf 0,$ the vector field $\mathbf F$ is not irrotational.

- Statement IV is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (counterclockwise), our thumb will point upward. Therefore, $\textrm{curl}\,\mathbf F$ points upward, in the direction of increasing $z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and IV only."

after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ x & 2y & 3z\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(3z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2y)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(3z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(x)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x)]k \\  & =(0-0)\,i-(0-0)\,j+(0-0)\,k \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Consider the vector field $F=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+y{z}^{2}\,j+(x-z)\,k.$ Evaluate $∇\times F$ at the point  $(2,-1,3).$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & y{z}^{2} & (x-z)\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{2})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{z}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))]k \\  & =(0-2yz)i-(1-0)j+(0-\frac{1}{x+y})k \\  & =-2yz\,i-j-\frac{1}{x+y}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\,F$ at the point $(2,-1,3),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(2,-1,3) & =-2(-1)(3)\,i-j-\frac{1}{2+(-1)}\,k \\  & =6\,i-j-k.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Consider the vector field $F=xy{e}^{z}\,j+yz{e}^{x}\,k.$ Evaluate $∇\times F$ at the point $(0,2,1).$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3},$ and the first partial derivatives exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field on ${R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 0 & xy{e}^{z} & yz{e}^{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(yz{e}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy{e}^{z})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(yz{e}^{x})-\frac{∂}{∂z}(0)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{z})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(0)]k \\  & =(z{e}^{x}-xy{e}^{z})i-(yz{e}^{x}-0)j+(y{e}^{z}-0)k \\  & =(z{e}^{x}-xy{e}^{z})\,i-yz{e}^{x}\,j+y{e}^{z}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\,F$ at the point $(0,2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(0,2,1) & =(1\cdot {e}^{0}-0\cdot 2\cdot {e}^{1})\,i-2\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0}\,j+2\cdot {e}^{1}\,k \\  & =i-2j+2e\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Consider the vector field $F=(2xy+2z)\,i+({y}^{2}+1)\,j+(x+y)\,k.$ Evaluate $∇\times F$ at the point  $(-3,0,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ 2xy+2z & {y}^{2}+1 & x+y\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+1)]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(2xy+2z)]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+1)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+2z)]k \\  & =(1-0)i-(1-2)j+(0-2x)k \\  & =\,i+j-2x\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\,F$ at the point $(-3,0,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(-3,0,-1) & =i+\,j-2(-3)\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+6\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y)=(x+{y}^{2})\,i+y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,j.$ Evaluate the scalar curl of $F$ at the point $(0,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1))-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1}-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the scalar curl at the point $(0,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})}_{(0,-1)} & =\frac{2(0)(-1)}{{0}^{2}+1}-2(-1) \\  & =0+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: Given that $F(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,i+(2x+3y)\,j,$ what is the scalar curl of $F?$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x+3y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =2-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Given that $F(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i+{e}^{xy}\,j,$ what is the scalar curl of $F?$
after.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the *scalar* curl of $F$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & =y{e}^{xy}-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y) \\  & =y{e}^{xy}+\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has a curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14108829/assets/86aee33cdfa96ac0a61468cc9657e791e399f31c024cdbc3a932193dc897d534.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statement I is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate clockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement III is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (counterclockwise), our thumb will point away from the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points away from the screen, in the direction of increasing $z.$

- Statement IV is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
